10374-the-ramblin-kid:
Earl Wayland Bowman published this western novel in 1920, with a frontispiece by W. H. D. Koerner. Its hero, the Ramblin' Kid, drifts into a town of bluffs, duels, and sweepstakes, where old Heck and other sharp dealers test his nerve. The title marks him as a wanderer who will not stay put.

A night letter, a bluff called, a duel of endurance, a dance and a ride, and the elite amusement parlor carry the plot through greed, pride, and revenge. Bowman writes in brisk, slangy western prose. Readers get a fast, colorful tale of cowboys, gamblers, and a young man who wins by staying cool.
13243-in-the-palace-of-the-king-a-love-s:
F. Marion Crawford's 1900 In the Palace of the King is a love story of old Madrid. It opens with two young girls in a high, narrow room of the Moorish palace Philip II made his capital's seat. It is November, light cold and grey, rain falling all morning, stones drying in patches. Crawford sets court love against Philip's stern Spain.

Don John lectures a young prince on Madrid as the wickedest, dirtiest habitation devised for corrupting man, especially in November, when hearts pack sins since Easter to unload at Christmas. Later, Mendoza finds a dead man with a bright spot on his doublet, no breath on a polished scabbard, and red drops from Philip's rapier. The novel is a rich, somber court romance.
1352-an-old-maid:
Honoré de Balzac tells of Mlle Cormon, a wealthy old maid of Alençon, whose fortune draws a pack of suitors, from a dashing officer to a miserly clerk. The tale follows her hopes, her blunders, and the marriage she at last makes, with provincial society watching every step.

Balzac writes Alençon with his usual wealth of detail, and his old maid is comic, touching, and all too human. The novel is a fine study of provincial life and the marriage market. It suits readers who like Balzac's comedies of money and love.
15541-what-two-children-did:
Charlotte E. Chittenden published this children's book in New York in 1903, with Hurst and Company. Twenty chapters follow two children, Ethelwyn and Beth, from a train journey on the way to the shore through dolls, weddings, plans, secrets, and rewards. A verse opening pictures the train's moving pictures, framed by earth and sky.

The story opens with Ethelwyn uneasy beside her mother, who sits thinking hard, two little lines between her eyes like sentinels. Beth asks whether God made a mistake in sending them here, and mistakes, easy to make, become a theme. Later chapters bring a lost invitation, a visit to grandmother's, and a chapter on how they bought a baby. The book is gentle family fiction, full of small adventures and kind lessons.
16253-madge-morton-captain-of-the-merry-:
Amy D. V. Chalmers's Madge Morton, Captain of the Merry Maid, published in Philadelphia by Henry Altemus in 1914, sends its heroine on a houseboat holiday. Madge plans the trip, chooses a chaperon, searches for a houseboat, and sets sail for Pleasure Bay, where an unknown jailer, an anxious night, and a girl on the island await. An exciting race, mercy of the waves, a brave fight, and life or death follow.

Madge comes into her own again and calls for help. She attempts a rescue and faces capture, a strange shore, and an evil genius. Mollie's brave fight and a farewell to the Merry Maid follow. Chalmers writes cheerful girls' adventure with pluck and friendship. Young readers will enjoy this sunny houseboat tale.
1639-eve-and-david:
Eve and David, part three of Balzac's Lost Illusions, returns the action to Angouleme, where Eve Sechard and her husband David face ruin. David's invention for cheap paper, Lucien's debts in Paris, and a conspiracy of rival printers and bankers threaten their press, their home, and their hopes.

Through lawsuits, forged bills, and a brother's return, Eve's steady courage holds the centre, and David's genius finds a bitter reward. The novel closes the trilogy with sorrow and a measure of grace. It is a powerful study of invention, debt, and a marriage tested by the world.
17342-the-motor-maid:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson, authors of Lord Loveland Discovers America and My Friend the Chauffeur, published this motoring novel in New York in August 1910, with colour pictures. The Williamsons were known for tales in which cars, roads, and travel drive the plot, and this book belongs to that run. An early picture shows a race along a clear road with a shining stretch of water ahead.

Readers get a romance of the open road from the first decade of motoring, when a car trip could still feel like an adventure. The story mixes travel, scenery, and society in the authors' easy, popular style. It suits readers curious about how the motor age first entered fiction, and how it changed the way novels moved their people about.
17381-what-timmy-did:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes's 1922 novel opens with a telephone bell ringing in the shabby, sunlit hall of Old Place, Beechfield, Surrey. Janet Tosswill, John's second wife, strips off gardening gloves to answer, puzzled that London wants them when no soul in London knows their number. Her dark hair, blue eyes, and Highland pride mark her at once.

From that wrong-number call grows a tale of a country parish, a Domesday past, and modern London pressing in. Lowndes writes in observant, suspenseful prose, with a psalm text on the sword and the dog at its head. Readers who like her mysteries will find a slow, atmospheric novel of home, marriage, and menace.
1846-the-vision-splendid:
A hero caught between an enemy's tactics, deserted friends, and a dubious cause talks his troubles over for hours with a woman who listens in his office. The hero, caught between the tactics of an enemy, the desertion of friends, and a dubious cause, discusses his troubles with a woman who listens for hours in his office.

The vision splendid of the title is the ideal that keeps him going when practical men desert him. Raine writes the western not as a gunfight but as a moral struggle. The book's interest lies in its hero's effort to hold a high aim in a world of compromises. It is a thoughtful entry in Raine's long shelf of outdoor tales.
19025-a-sweet-little-maid:
Amy E. Blanchard wrote this 1899 story for girls about Dimple, a sweet little maid, and her friend Florence. Dimple plays with dolls, quarrels, makes up, and shares tea upstairs with her doll Bubbles waiting on them. The book is dedicated to the author's goddaughter Agnes.

Tea by the window, wistaria peeping in, and a brown bird on the sill set the tone of gentle home play. Florence envies Dimple's quiet house, while Dimple admires Florence's tall town house and fine things. Young readers get a soft, old-style tale of friendship, dolls, and small daily joys.
20186-the-dismal-swamp-and-lake-drummond:
The Dismal Swamp and Lake Drummond recalls early efforts to use Virginia's great swamp. George Washington held land there through the Dismal Swamp Land Company. After the Revolutionary War, that company set hands to cutting timber. A large amount of timber was cut and readied for sale.

Yet the timber needed an outlet that swamp roads could not give. Only a canal or ditch could float it out to buyers. Washington thus backed ditch and canal work in the swamp's heart. Readers get local history mixed with vivid, amusing scenes from swamp life.
20512-man-and-maid:
Elinor Glyn's novel Man and Maid opens in the voice of a soldier broken by the Great War. He looks at his mutilated face before he puts the black patch over his left eye. His shoulder is crooked, and his right leg is gone from the knee down.

With such a wreck of a man, he believes, no woman can feel emotion for him again in this world. The novel tests that despair against love. Glyn, famous for romantic fiction, writes here about wounds that show and wounds that hide, in the hard years just after the war.
20678-the-tory-maid:
Herbert Baird's The Tory Maid, published in 1898, is a romance of the American Revolution in Maryland. The narrator writes as an old man, looking back on the wild days of his youth. He settles on the great porch of Fairlee to tell his story, with old friends around him.

With a julep on his right hand and the paper before him, he takes up the pen. He writes of the days when he first drew his sword in the Great Cause. The maid of the title holds Tory loyalties, and love across the divide drives the tale Baird builds.
21275-the-goat-and-her-kid:
Mrs Harriet Myrtle's stories for young children were issued in New York in 1870 in the Rose-Bud Stories series. They open on a bright green grass plot behind a cottage. A goat nibbles there all day with her pretty kid running at her side. But this kid loves dancing and frisking more than any kid in the village.

A poor Italian boy comes down the lane playing a pipe and tabor for two dancing dolls, and the kid's adventures begin. Other tales in the little book include one on young birds tumbling from the nest and a final piece, Winter Pleasures. Myrtle wrote simply, for the youngest readers.
22047-the-love-affairs-of-an-old-maid:
Lilian Bell published The Love Affairs of an Old Maid in 1893 under a teasing title. Her narrator is a spinster who reviews, with dry honesty, the loves of her life. She admits she dares to be brutally frank only with herself. To the world she keeps a proper face, but on paper nothing is spared.

Each affair is recalled in turn, with its hopes, blunders, and quiet endings. Bell writes bright, chatty comedy rather than tragedy. The book plays with the idea that an "old maid" may have had more romance than her married friends. It was light reading with a sharp edge, popular in the 1890s.
22538-the-devil-s-asteroid:
Manly Wade Wellman wrote The Devil's Asteroid, a science fiction adventure of space exile. A skipper with a rolling accent lands his ship under orders. Prisoners get thirty seconds, Earth time, to clear the blast.

Now we ground, the skipper announces as the shock comes. The inner panel opens, then the outer hatch, into beating sunlight. Goodbye, he says formally to the man put ashore alone. Thirty seconds to walk clear before the ship takes off again. That cruel farewell launches the stranded man's fight to survive. An asteroid that works as a prison gives the tale its title. Readers get pulp space adventure with a lone convict's odds.
23045-measure-for-measure-the-works-of-w:
The Duke hands over Vienna in Measure for Measure, printed here from the Cambridge Shakespeare. The Duke declines to lecture Angelo on ruling. Angelo's own knowledge of government, he says, passes any counsel he could offer. Nothing remains but to let that competence do its work.

What Angelo does with that power drives Shakespeare's darkest comedy. Puritan strictness meets its own appetites, and the disguised Duke watches his city from the shadows. The Cambridge editors' notes track the text's early printings in their usual detail. Of all the plays here, this one argues hardest with its audience. Justice, mercy, and desire each get measured, and none comes out exact.
23558-the-samuel-butler-collection-at-sa:
Henry Festing Jones and A. T. Bartholomew catalogued the Samuel Butler collection at Saint John's College, Cambridge, in a nineteen twenty one Heffer edition limited to seven hundred and fifty copies. Butler's own line opens the book. A true life lies not in the self one knows, but in the life one lives in the hearts of others, with bodies and brains as mere tools for that work.

Contents list pictures, sketches, and drawings by or about Butler, books and music he wrote, books about him, books relating to him and his subjects, and books once his property. The catalogue serves scholars of Erewhon, The Way of All Flesh, and Butler's quarrels with Darwin. Readers who collect or study Butler will value the careful record of what Cambridge holds, and the commentary that sets each item in a life's work.
24493-the-boy-who-knew-what-the-birds-sa:
Padraic Colum wrote this book of Irish wonder tales, published by Macmillan in 1918 with pictures by Dugald Stewart Walker. A boy learns what the birds say, and their talk opens a world of giants, kings, and magic. The contents list a stone of victory, a castle, and a hero called Feet-in-the-Ashes.

Colum retells old Irish stories in clear, musical prose, keeping their strangeness and their humour. Birds warn, mock, and guide the boy through dangers no grown man could face alone. Young readers get a beautiful doorway into Irish folklore, told by a poet who loved the tales and knew how to tell them.
24608-the-tale-of-kiddie-katydid:
Kiddie Katydid stars in this Tuck-Me-In Tale by Arthur Scott Bailey, published at New York by Grosset and Dunlap with pictures by Harry L. Smith. The series also tells of Jolly Robin, Old Mr. Crow, Solomon Owl, Jasper Jay, Rusty Wren, and Daddy Long-Legs, all small creatures of field and garden.

A frontispiece picture shows Kiddie seeing Benjamin Bat in front of the moon. Bailey's short chapters follow the katydid through summer nights, with gentle humour for bedtime. Small children get a musical insect story, told in the simple style that made Bailey's animal books favourites.
2709-the-man-who-was-afraid:
Maxim Gorky wrote this novel as Foma Gordyeff, here translated by Herman Bernstein, and the English title calls its hero the man who was afraid. An introductory note hails Gorky as the poet of the vagabond and the proletariat, a Byron of the twentieth century risen from life's darkest depths.

Foma, heir to a merchant fortune, fears the life laid out for him and rebels against money, vice, and respectability. Gorky writes with fierce sympathy for outcasts and misfits. The novel endures as a portrait of a soul refusing its inheritance, and of Russia on the edge of change.
28045-walls-of-acid:
Henry Hasse wrote Walls of Acid, a science-fiction story set five thousand years after Diskra rid itself of the loathsome Termans. The tale opens far beneath a city, where Braanol, a huge brain in tanks of liquid, stirs from aeons of sleep as imperial messengers enter his room.

Braanol lowers his thought-potential to speak kindly with the frightened visitors, learning that Empress Alaazar is long dead and Empress Uldulla now reigns. The story asks what other planets hold, and it blends space adventure with the strange figure of a disembodied intelligence kept alive for counsel.
28110-jimsy-the-christmas-kid:
Leona Dalrymple's Jimsy: The Christmas Kid, published in New York in October 1915, is a holiday story for young readers. Jimsy, a thin city boy, arrives in a New England village two days before Christmas, full of noise and hope. His host, Abner Sawyer, a thrifty first citizen, fears the boy will upset a plain, unadorned Christmas.

Chapters follow a chain of small deeds, from a biscuit link to a triumph and a downfall, as Jimsy wins over the village. Charles Guischard drew the decorations. The tale praises warmth, giving, and faith in something wonderful, against mere thrift.
29257-the-book-of-khalid:
Ameen Rihani published this novel in New York in 1911 with Dodd, Mead and Company. It carries illustrations by Khalil Gibran, author of The Prophet. The Book of Khalid is an early Arab-American novel. Its contents show its shape: Book the First, In the Exchange, runs from probing the trivial through the city of Baal and the Via Dolorosa to the cellar of the soul.

Book the Second, In the Temple, moves through the dowry of democracy, the false dawn, and the last star. Rihani writes in a lyrical, philosophical voice about a man between worlds. Readers get a pioneering work of Arab-American literature, rich in imagery and ideas, that still rewards readers tracing the immigrant imagination.
29457-loot-of-the-void:
Edwin K. Sloat's tale, printed in Astounding Stories in September 1932, sends Dick Penrun after the hidden hoard of Halkon, a feared space pirate of the Void. Aboard the Western Star, bound for the Martian city of Nurm, Penrun meets Lozzo, a Martian who claims he once sailed as Halkon's cabin boy. Lozzo is one hundred and seventy-five years old, and Martians, he says, may live three centuries.

Penrun follows the trail to a trap-door city of great spiders, where greed meets real peril. Sloat mixes dice games, shipboard talk, and sudden danger with the wide romance of early space pulp. Readers get a fast, colorful yarn in which old treasure, strange beasts, and a long-lived witness drive the chase.
29752-an-orkney-maid:
Amelia E. Barr, author of Christine, Joan, and Profit and Loss, wrote An Orkney Maid, printed by D. Appleton and Company of New York. Its chapters run from an introduction and the house of Ragnor through Adam Vedder's trouble, Aries the Ram, and Sunna and her grandfather, to Sunna and Thora and the old, old trouble. A picture shows Ian utterly charmed with the picture she made.

Barr writes of Orkney life with the warmth of a novelist who loved islands and their folk. Kind voices round a fireside open the tale, speaking the mother tongue of home. Readers of Barr and of Scottish island fiction will find a gentle, heartfelt novel of family, sea, and the north.
2996-the-romantic-adventures-of-a-milkma:
Thomas Hardy's tale The Romantic Adventures of a Milkmaid opens at half past four on a May morning in the eighteen forties. Its authority is a land surveyor with the faintest curve of humor on his lips. A dense white fog hangs over the Valley of the Exe, ending against the hills, while sounds from below tell of bustling life invisible from higher ground. The milkmaid Margery meets Jim on a little bridge.

He raps his stick on the rail, seats himself firmly, and demands a straightforward answer about the month and day she will marry him. Margery coaxes that she wants to get home, while Jim insists on an answer. The tale charms as a Wessex romance, with fog, a bridge, and a proposal pressed in the open air.
3016-what-diantha-did:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote What Diantha Did as a novel about a young woman who turns housekeeping into a profession. The story opens at the Warden house, impressive with grounds, pillared porches, galleries, and a cupola, yet covered with heavy flowering vines and heavy mortgages. Mrs. Roscoe Warden and four daughters repose under the vines while Roscoe Warden Junior struggles under the mortgages.

Diantha, an arithmetical young woman, proposes to run housework as a business, with trained workers, fair wages, and efficient methods. Her employers marvel that she makes them feel they pay in wampum instead of money, mere primitive barter for twentieth-century service. The novel argues Gilman's feminist economics through story, and it remains her most practical fiction.
31897-you-don-t-make-wine-like-the-greek:
David E. Fisher's short story You Don't Make Wine Like the Greeks Did opens in a small office on the Empire State Building's sixty-third floor. It holds a receptionist, three rather uncomfortable armchairs, and a disorderly mixture of Life, Look, and New Yorker magazines. Its hero Donald Fairfield drives out to Long Island with Dr. Quink, quiet at the wheel of his new Buick, fighting and coasting with the eastbound traffic.

An illustration caption promises the heart of the tale: Donald is determined to make Mimi go back to their world, dead or alive. Readers get a science-fiction story of two worlds and a stubborn lover, told with a wry eye for modern offices, cars, and manners.
32162-the-beasts-in-the-void:
Paul W. Fairman's short story, printed in Imagination in April 1956, turns a space hunting trip into madness. Its tagline notes that Holloway knew big-game hunters and off-world expeditions well, yet this voyage was pure madness, a spaceship hunting among beasts. The story opens after the fact, with an examiner who doubts Holloway and insists that regulations require reading his log before taking verbal testimony.

Holloway's face is drawn and ravaged, his bloodshot eyes sitting in black pits, trained on the examiner but looking through him rather than at him. He must talk, he insists, and keep talking. It started in the control cabin in deep space, he says, when Mrs. Kelvey came in, the blonde one, and told him: Captain, there is a great big tiger in the companionway. Readers get a space-horror tale of a hunt that hunts back.
32686-day-of-the-druid:
Knut Enferd tells of Gaar, a seven-foot Northman of thirty who chafes at fog-bound days in the great hall. Old sailor Vornung recalls Picts met after a storm, a hairy folk in skins who told tales of treasure and a beautiful woman held in endless sleep by her people's priests.

Gaar sails south to test the tale and finds the Picts ready to fight, swarming aboard his ship under cover of dark. Battles, a duel with the tricky Glendyn, and a veiled sleeper in a hidden place follow, as Gaar seeks both the treasure and the woman kept by the god Be'al. Gaar wants deeds, not tales. The fog only sharpens his hunger for action.
33028-man-and-maid:
E. Nesbit's Man and Maid, published in London in 1906, gathers stories that mix the everyday with the uncanny. Its contents run from The Haunted Inheritance and The Power of Darkness through The Stranger Who Might Have Been Observed and Rack and Thumbscrew. They go on to The Millionairess, The Hermit of the Yews, and The Aunt and the Editor. Later tales include Miss Mouse, The House of Silence, and Alcibiades.

Nesbit, known for The Treasure Seekers and Five Children and It, brings her gift for domestic magic to adult readers here. Haunted houses, strange strangers, and quiet heroines carry stories that are witty as well as eerie. The collection suits readers who enjoy a tale that starts in a drawing room and slips, gently or suddenly, into something stranger. It is a charming, varied volume from a master storyteller.
35849-an-old-story-of-my-farming-days-vo:
An Old Story of My Farming Days, in German Ut Mine Stromtid, is a novel by Fritz Reuter, translated by Macdowall. This first volume of three appeared in the Tauchnitz Collection of German Authors, at Leipzig in 1878. The Tauchnitz editions carried Continental fiction to English readers across Europe.

Reuter wrote of Mecklenburg country life in hard times. His narrator insists that the country people did not hobble about like scarecrows, nor could a prayer be read through their sunken cheeks. They were true Mecklenburgers every bit, he says, for all their poverty. The novel, written first in Low German, became the most beloved prose work in that tongue: a humorous, tender chronicle of farming folk, bailiffs and small-town life in the north German plain. Tauchnitz sold each volume separately, this one as volume thirty four of the collection.
35850-an-old-story-of-my-farming-days-vo:
An Old Story of My Farming Days is a novel by Fritz Reuter, here in Volume Two of three. Bernhard Tauchnitz of Leipzig issued it in his Collection of German Authors, as Volume Thirty-Five of that series. Macdowall translated it from the German. Its home title is Ut Mine Stromtid, out of my farming days.

The tale is a servant's and farmer's chronicle of old Mecklenburg. Its narrator looks back on masters, inns, and harvests with a sly, warm eye. In one scene a farmer takes the boy into the inn's sitting-room, shows him his wife, and calls her the lad's new mistress. She gives him a glass of wine, and he worries that he looked a little foolish. Reuter, the great Low German novelist, builds his comedy from such small change of rural life.
35851-an-old-story-of-my-farming-days-vo:
An Old Story of My Farming Days, volume three, is the last part of Fritz Reuter's novel Ut Mine Stromtid, translated from the German by Macdowall. The authorised edition was printed at Leipzig in 1878 by Tauchnitz, in his collection of German authors. Reuter wrote in the Low German of Mecklenburg, and his farming story is beloved there as a classic.

The volume opens the day after Christmas, in the house of Mrs. Behrens at Rahnstaedt. Louisa runs up and down stairs, finishing the arrangement of her father's room. Each time she thinks it perfect she finds some small thing to improve. Dinner time comes, but her father has not arrived. Reuter's art is in such scenes: the talk, the waiting, the small hopes of country people, told with humour and exact knowledge of the farming world he grew up in.
37922-the-indians-last-fight-or-the-dull:
Dennis Collins published his frontier memoir The Indians' Last Fight, or the Dull Knife Raid, with the Appeal to Reason press at Girard, Kansas. His twenty-nine chapters run from the Santa Fe Trail and freighting days through cattle round-ups, wild-horse catching, and the hard times of the early settlements. The later chapters turn to war: the Messiah Craze, the Adobe Wall raid, and the Dull Knife raid itself.

Collins writes as a witness rather than a historian. He recalls postmasters of the early days, a cowboy love affair, the visit of Sheridan, and the capture of Comanches and Kiowas. His first chapter sets the tone, contrasting the settler, digging his well and storm cave, with the half of the world that never asks how the other half lives. The book preserves a settler's memory of the last Plains wars.
38039-history-of-billy-the-kid:
Chas A Siringo tells an outlaw's life in the History of Billy the Kid, copyrighted in 1920. The title page bills its subject as a cowboy outlaw whose youthful daring has never been equalled in the annals of criminal history. When Sheriff Pat Garett's bullet pierced his heart he was under twenty-two, with twenty-one men killed, Indians not counted.

The tale starts in a New York slum on November 23, 1859, where blue-eyed Billy Bonney was born to William H Bonney and his wife Kathleen. The family drifted to Kansas, Colorado, and Santa Fe, and the boy grew up among gamblers in Silver City.
40005-north-american-recent-soft-shelled:
North American Recent Soft-shelled Turtles, by Robert Webb, was published by the University of Kansas in February 1962. The study fills more than a hundred and eighty pages, with plates and figures. Webb sets out his collecting methods, his materials, and his way of working before he turns to naming.

The naming part treats the family, then the genus Trionyx. He works through change by sex, by age, and by place, and weighs the traits that split one kind from another. A made key leads to each North American kind and subkind. Full accounts follow, species by species. Readers get a deep museum study for anyone who needs to name a soft-shelled turtle with care.
41125-mr-jacobs-a-tale-of-the-drummer-th:
Mr Jacobs is a comic tale of a drummer, a reporter, and a conjurer. Clarke and Carruth published the seventh edition at Boston in 1883. The book delights in absurd, tangled sentences. Its first page parodies philosophic prose. Long clauses pile qualification on qualification. A footnote confesses that the editor cut twenty pages.

The narrator sits at tiffin and studies a stranger. The man drinks water from a goblet cut from one emerald. He swallows without wincing, a phenomenon to the watcher. Free-lunch neighbours gorge beside him by contrast. The stranger's eyes are jewels of six precious stones. A hundred generations of Persian magi seem pent within them. The narrator addresses him in Gaelic. He answers in two words of modern Hebrew.
428-frivolous-cupid:
Anthony Hope, writing as Sir Anthony Hope Hawkins, gathers eight light tales of love and marriage in this volume. Young men home from school, lawn-tennis clubs, and country houses set the scenes. Suitors dither, change heart, repent, and marry by compulsion, all under Cupid's teasing rule.

The opening tale follows Harry Sterling, back from Harrow and bound for Oxford, as old playmates greet him as a new man. Later stories weigh why men shun marriage and how a firm heart may still win. Hope writes with wit and ease, and the book reads as a graceful comedy of courtship.
4396-the-woman-who-did:
Grant Allen wrote this brief, controversial novel in 1895, dedicating it to his wife and to a less fortunate love. He wrote it at Perugia in the spring of 1893, for the first time wholly to satisfy his own taste and conscience. His preface frames the story as an answer to a friend who doubted any woman would dare to do what his heroine does.

The woman who did is Herminia Barton, who lives by her principles on free love and motherhood outside marriage, and pays the price society exacts. Allen's novel became a byword of the New Woman debate. It remains a frank, polemical book, admired and attacked in its day for treating a woman's sexual freedom as a moral claim.
440-just-david:
Eleanor Porter tells of David, a boy raised alone with his father in a mountain shack, in this gentle novel. David knows music, nature, and his father's violin, but little of town ways. When his father dies, David must come down to the valley and learn its puzzling dos and don'ts among strangers.

Porter follows David through discords, nuisances, and small rescues, as his music softens hard hearts. A lady of roses, a tower window, and a castle in Spain fill his dreams. The book charms as a warm tale of innocence meeting the world, and of beauty found in plain things.
45168-rhymes-for-harry-and-his-nurse-mai:
Rhymes for Harry and His Nurse-Maid was printed in London by William Darton and Son. A mother wrote the verses and says so with humility. A front verse states the plan: a simple tale in rhyme can teach a lesson. Her preface aims hints at nurse maids and young mothers. Middle class mothers, she notes, have little time to study child care. Early habits matter most, in her view.

The first three years, she argues, lay the base for later life. A child's will should be ruled by mild yet firm conduct. Self will left to root brings lasting sorrow. Plates show a nurse's first thoughts and a pin that pricked the baby. Notes carry the practical counsel behind the rhymes.
457-the-price-she-paid:
David Graham Phillips opens this novel with the death of Henry Gower, a man praised as generous yet selfish to the core. His widow and children, kept in luxury for his own comfort, find he saved nothing for them. His daughter must now face the world with beauty, pride, and little cash.

Phillips follows her through suitors, stages, and bargains as she learns what each choice costs. The price of the title is paid in pride, love, and years. The novel reads as a sharp study of a family built on a fraud, and of a woman who must earn her own worth.
45982-the-boy-allies-in-the-baltic-or-th:
Ensign Robert Drake wrote this Boy Allies tale of war in the Baltic. Burt printed it in New York in 1916, one of a famed set. Lord Hastings commands the British submarine D-17 on a raid. Jack Templeton serves as its first officer, a British youth.

Frank Chadwick, an American youth, stands second officer of the craft. Hastings orders a dive to five fathoms, then ten, fast. Engine room trouble stands repaired as the raid plan firms. A front plate shows Jack lashing wolves with his whip on ice. Past Boy Allies books under the sea and on patrol stand named on the title page.
46956-ned-the-son-of-webb-what-he-did:
William Stoddard's Ned, the Son of Webb: What He Did was published by Dana Estes of Boston in 1900, with pictures by Searles. Stoddard had written Crowded Out o' Crofield before it. The contents promise a boy's tale that runs from modern warships to the Norman conquest: the great Fulford fight, Harold the Saxon, Stamford Bridge, and the battle of Senlac.

Chapter one, The War Spirit, opens at Pier Number One on the North River. Ned and Uncle Jack watch the battleship Kentucky steam slowly up the stream, her double turrets tall as a house. Ned is sure she could knock any other ironclad in the world; Uncle Jack is glad she is out of range of them. The talk of keels of the Northland and scouting parties ahead sets the boy dreaming himself back into 1066.
47372-for-love-of-a-bedouin-maid:
For Love of a Bedouin Maid, by the writer called Le Voleur, was published at Chicago and New York in 1897. The introduction opens in London, on the night of July 22, 1893. Lord Throgmorten, about thirty six, stout, with reddish hair and steel gray eyes, has just come home from a yachting cruise.

He had taken his title about eighteen months before. In his Albany chambers he orders cigars set on the table. With him is Percival Phelps, a genial, dapper little clerk, his guest on the cruise, vain and with a slight stammer when excited. The contents point to a fourth epoch, headed Captive, But Emperor Still. Readers get a sensational romance that moves from London rooms toward captivity and the Bedouin maid of the title.
50022-the-wailing-asteroid:
Murray Leinster wrote this space mystery as an Avon paperback original in 1960. The Wailing Asteroid opens on a dead world with a live signal. Miles of rock-hewn halls run through the asteroid, and their purpose is plain at a look.

The place is a mighty fortress. Weapons of ruin past man's grasp stock its rooms. Yet no life stands here, nor has for untold ages. What race built this stronghold? What vast power were they set against? Why was it left? No answer comes; all is dead. But not quite all. In a room above the fort a strong sender beams its fluting, birdlike sounds toward Earth. On a star map by it, ten tiny red sparks crawl toward their mark.
50827-orphans-of-the-void:
Orphans of the Void is a science fiction story by Michael Shaara, with illustrations by a named artist, printed in a magazine in June 1952. A line at the head sets its theme before the tale begins. Finding a cause worth dying for is no great trick, it says, since the universe is full of them. Finding one worth living for is the genuine problem.

The story opens in the region of a dark nebula, on the dead fourth planet of a star. A captain of the Mapping Command stands counting buildings: eleven, then twelve. He wonders if the number holds any meaning, and admits he has no idea. His second in command, in a spacesuit, guesses the place is a temporary camp built of native stuff. Castaways, he suggests, as they climb to a flat of weathered stone.
52244-mail-carrying-railways-underpaid:
Mail Carrying Railways Underpaid is a rail trade plea issued in October nineteen hundred twelve. The Committee on Railway Mail Pay speaks for two hundred sixty eight firms in it. Their lines ran two hundred fourteen thousand two hundred seventy five miles in all. J Kruttschnitt of the Union Pacific chaired the group.

Mail pay, the roads charge, fails to meet the costs it makes. No cent is left as gain on the road wealth used. The Postmaster General claimed roads were overpaid about $9,000,000 in nineteen hundred nine. That claim rests on a new rule, the roads reply. It grants no gain at all on the wealth sunk in plant. Space counts short changed mail cars in his sums too, they add. Parcel post, due January first next, will swell mail loads at once.
53127-san-xavier-del-bac-arizona-a-descr:
Workers of the Writers' Program of the Work Projects Administration in Arizona compiled this guide to Mission San Xavier del Bac, first published in March 1940. The Arizona Pioneers' Historical Society sponsored it, and Hastings House of New York printed it. The title promises both description and history, and the book is full of photographs.

Pictures show the facade, the front view, the bells, the courtyard from above and below, and the high altar from several sides. A Papago village and Papago children appear among the plates. The editors thank Herbert Bolton of the Bancroft Library for help with the history, and they lean on Prent Duell's work for the account of the building.
53711-the-orchid:
The Orchid is a novel by Robert Grant, printed by Charles Scribner Sons in New York in 1905, with plates by Alonzo Kimball. Grant centers the tale on Lydia Arnold, a woman of quick mind and dry voice. The front plate shows a toast to the loveliest woman in creation.

Lydia grasps the sense of what is said to her at once, yet pauses a beat before she speaks. Her words come out neat, clear, and cool, with no heat in them. Yet she laughs with ease and is far from grave. Her father, kind but self bent, died in her youth and left her training loose. Readers meet a sharp study of a modern woman, her talk, her pride, and her place in fine society.
53795-the-prince-of-the-house-of-david:
The Prince of the House of David, by the Reverend J H Ingraham, appears here as number seven of the first volume of the New Sabbath Library. David C Cook Publishing Company of Chicago and Elgin issued the monthly in October 1898 at five cents a copy, or sixty cents a year. The Library had begun in April 1898 to meet the demand for pure literature at popular prices.

Each number held a complete story in ninety-six large pages of double columns, in clear type with half-tone engravings. Ingraham's biblical novel, the life of Christ told in a narrative of his own house and people, was already one of the famous books of its class. Cook's series aimed its wholesome stories particularly at young people. Cloth editions at twenty-five cents were offered for presentation.
54504-master-and-maid:
Mrs L Allen Harker wrote a novel copyrighted in 1910, set in a school house at Hamchester College. Anthony Bevan, called Bruiser Bevan, is housemaster of B House. On the second Friday of term he sits at dessert with three prefects. They talk over football prospects and holiday news over walnuts and light port.

A carriage crunches on the new gravel, and a young lady bursts in unannounced. She says her father promised to telegraph but forgot, as usual. Val, the Irish terrier under the master's chair, leaps on her in delight. The girl is nineteen, small, slim, and pale. Her voice gives her force when she speaks.
55019-historical-record-of-the-fifteenth:
Richard Cannon compiled this record of the Fifteenth, or the Yorkshire East Riding, Regiment of Foot, printed in London in 1848. It gives the making of the regiment in 1685 and its services after, to 1848. Plates go with the text. It stands in a run of such records, made from the Adjutant-General's office.

The regimental colour bears two names, Martinique and Guadaloupe. They mark the taking of those islands in 1809 and 1810. Contents run by years. The regiment is raised at Nottingham in 1685 and camped on Hounslow Heath. The upheaval of 1688 sends it to Scotland. The battle of Killiecrankie in 1689 and Cromdale follow. In 1694 it ships for Flanders and is engaged in the taking of Huy. The surrender of Dixmude, and a colonel cashiered, stand in the tale. The peace at Ryswick closes the early run.
56106-john-brown-s-raid:
John Brown's Raid is a handbook of the National Park Service History Series, issued by the United States Department of the Interior. Staff of the Office of Publications prepared the text. It rests on Park Service reports by William C Everhart and Arthur L Sullivan. A picture of John Brown's Fort at Harpers Ferry illustrates the opening.

Chapters trace the road to Harpers Ferry and the rendezvous for revolution. To Free the Slaves states Brown's aim in his own generation's terms. The Tiger Caged and The Trap Is Sprung carry the raid to its end. John Brown's Body and an epilogue close the story. An appendix treats the capture of John Brown, and a reading list follows. Park handbooks were made to be read before, during, and after a visit. This one keeps interpretation tight and documented at a charged site.
57531-mermaid:
Grant M Overton wrote the novel Mermaid for Doubleday, Page at Garden City in 1920, with a front plate by Henry A Botkin. He dedicated the tale to Gene Stratton-Porter. Part one opens in a quarrel between Keturah Smiley and her brother.

Keturah snaps that no one can play Providence to a married couple. Her brother answers that some women can play Lucifer, and denies blame for his wife's flight. A little girl of about six, saved from the wreck of the Mermaid, has been taken in by the men at the life-saving station. They call her Mermaid, since no one knows her name. A sea wreck and a nameless child open Overton's romance.
59113-the-luck-of-the-kid:
Ridgwell Cullum wrote The Luck of the Kid, a novel of the far north published by Putnam's Sons in 1923. Cullum had earlier written The Heart of Unaga and The Man in the Twilight. He dedicated this, his twenty-first book, to his brothers, in memory of their early boyhood.

The story opens north of sixty in the heat of a sub-Arctic summer, where two men sit on a river bank. Chapters move through fire, plotting, and vengeance, then shift to Placer City and a reindeer farm. The Valley of the Fire Hills, a dream hill, and the end of the long trail carry the tale to its close. Cullum mixes gold-country adventure with the harsh weather and strong loyalties of the northern frontier.
59486-ely-s-automatic-housemaid:
Ely's Automatic Housemaid is a story by Elizabeth Bellamy. The narrator tells of Harrison Ely, a college friend of his, a genius of a strange kind. Ely was dull at Latin, Greek, and even English, the narrator says, but full of mechanical ideas he could not put into words. His self-acting lexicon holder won the wonder of his classmates.

His self-feeding safety lamp lit everything for him except the path to a degree. Years later the narrator meets Ely's newest invention, the automatic housemaid of the title. The tale plays the inventor's gift against his failures in ordinary life. It is a light story of Yankee ingenuity and its limits.
59752-the-moon-maid:
Edgar Burroughs wrote this tale of the Moon Maid and Mars Day. Munsey printed it at New York, copyright 1923, prologue first. The scene opens June 10, 1967, aboard the liner Harding. A half century of war since 1914 has ended at last.

Anglo Saxon rule stands absolute over all races of the world. Arms and ammunition sink into the five oceans for peace now. Air fleets turn to carriers for trade and calm commerce there. The narrator takes the one free chair by a smiling stranger. Victory Day two months before had seemed past all matching in the world joy.
60399-thomas-reid:
Thomas Reid is a biography by Campbell Fraser in the Famous Scots Series, printed at Edinburgh by Oliphant, Anderson, and Ferrier. Sister volumes treat Carlyle, Burns, Hume, and Scott. The contents run from boyhood at Strachan to Reid's place in the nineteenth century.

Reid was born on April 26, 1710, in the manse of Strachan in Kincardineshire, where his father was minister for fifty eight years. He studied at Marischal College, held a parish at New Machar, and knew David Hume. In 1764 his Inquiry into the Human Mind set inspired common sense against universal scepticism. Glasgow then made him professor of moral philosophy, and his last years went to writing in retirement.
61430-manners-and-customs-of-the-thrid:
Manners and Customs of the Thrid, by Murray Leinster, was produced from Worlds of If Science Fiction for September 1963. A head line calls the Thrid the wisest creatures in space: they even said so themselves. The trouble, the text opens, was that Jorgenson saw things as a business man does.

But also, contradictorily, he saw them as right and just, or as wrong and intolerable. As a business man, he should have kept his mind on business and never bothered about Ganti. As a believer in right and wrong, he would have been wiser to stay off the planet Thriddar altogether. He woke thinking of Ganti, in a bad mood. Most humans wanted weapons, which the Thrid did not use, to change the local system. Readers get a Leinster alien contact tale built on clashing morals.
61978-war-gods-of-the-void:
War-Gods of the Void is a science fiction story by Henry Kuttner, printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1942. Jerry Vanning, an earth state investigator, has trailed the fugitive Callahan to Venus. The Earth Consul, Goodenow, tells him he is crazy. Only fools come to Venus, and the man he wants is not there.

Vanning checks passport microfilms anyway, through the headache the Venusian air gives him. Callahan, he explains, began as a diplomat and found it too quiet. He stole a secret treaty that could start a revolution, above all on Callisto. Vanning means to find him before he shows it in the right places. The tale promises the swampy wastes of Venus and the fabled War-Gods beyond them, pulp adventure of the planetary kind.
62040-monster-of-the-asteroid:
Ray Cummings's Monster of the Asteroid appeared in Planet Stories in the winter of 1941. Its teaser speaks of two new slaves of the Master of a pitted Devil's Isle in outer space, gambling where win or lose the take is death. The story begins on a summer evening in 1965.

The narrator sits with Dora Franklin at an outdoor concert, under strings of coloured tubelights. A cloaked, hawk-nosed man sidles onto their bench and stares at Dora, while his companion lurks in the shadows nearby. The companion seems no more than five feet tall, wrapped in a long black overcoat. Worse, the top of the coat sags limp, as though the thing inside it had no head at all.
62324-grifters-asteroid:
Grifters' Asteroid, by H L Gold, first appeared in Planet Stories in May 1943. Harvey and Joe were the slickest con-men ever to gyp a space-lane sucker, or so they thought. Angus Johnson knew differently, and charged them five buckos for a glass of water, and got it.

Harvey Ellsworth keeps his dignity though his tongue hangs out, while Joe Mallon lurches across the rubbish-strewn patch called a spaceport on Planetoid 42. Inside the battered metalloy saloon, a six-armed native carries liquor, siphons, and a broom all at once, taking orders from the bartender.
62350-mutiny-in-the-void:
Charles Tanner stages a ship revolt in Mutiny in the Void, from the Fall 1943 issue of Planet Stories. The rocket ship Berenice draws her air from tanks of water weed. Manool Sarouk, the dapper farm chief, keeps that farm in fine trim.

The blurb gives his wild plan away. To break the mutiny, Manool destroys the plants that furnish oxygen for the whole ship. The tale opens in the tank room, bright and clean, with bubbles that rise from the weed. Manool is proud of his work and his looks. Then he steps in with terror and dread on his face. Air itself turns to a weapon in this brisk space tale.
63518-vandals-of-the-void:
Robert Wilson wrote Vandals of the Void, a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1945. Its opening is grim. The void has spawned hell-creatures of destruction and sown them deep in Earth's soil. Now Earth reaps a whirlwind of death, and human weapons prove futile against immortal conquerors from another space.

Art Douglas sees one of the first creatures. Two drivers from a huge steel burrowing worm bring it up from explorations far below the Kansas prairies. The thing lies on his laboratory bench at the Interplanetary Research Institute. Douglas first assumes the creature-plants belong to the deep level where they were found. He is terribly wrong. The organism plainly bores through solid rock, and its powers point to a menace he cannot yet dream of. Wilson's tale is pulp science fiction of the war years, built on a buried invasion discovered too late.
64725-valkyrie-from-the-void:
Basil Wells wrote Valkyrie from the Void, a science fiction tale printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1948. The head line follows the priestess Ylda, staggering under a great ringed sun across her savage, slimy world. Her goal, the blurb promises, lies bright and shining a thousand light-years away, though she does not know it.

The tale opens with Hardan Synn riding home. His mount is a graceful golden-furred maar, and three fat Dryland birds hang from his hornless saddle. Five years of roaming the blistering plains with prospectors have spoiled his taste for camp fare. From the river bluff he hears the camp erupt: men fighting, fists and clubs smashing, screams rising over the muddy water. Nitka Porn again, he spits, always stirring trouble among the sarifs. Wells mixes the sword-and-planet camp with a quest laid across the stars.
66211-x-marks-the-asteroid:
X Marks the Asteroid, a science fiction tale by Ross Rocklynne, ran in Imagination in January 1954. Far in space, Ralph's kin lie in deep sleep with a price on their heads. They left him a map and a hard choice: wake them, or take the reward for their capture.

Word that the Unterzuyder map is out of hiding races across the planets and lands in Marsport. A crime boss named Bigger Bailes vows to claim reward money that has grown for eighty-five years in a New York bank. Ralph, he says, hides under the name Carruthers Straley and has formed a settler group bound for Titan. Greed, disguise, and family duty drive the chase.
66396-danger-in-the-void:
Danger in the Void is a science fiction tale by Charles Fritch. It ran in Imagination Stories in August of the year 1954. A blurb says Silvia secretly planned to divorce George at Arcturus. A space journey can alter a careful plan, or hatch a worse one. Trouble starts when the Arcturus Queen is four billion miles out.

The ship pulls clear of the solar system on conventional drive first. Then it switches into subspace for the long haul to the star. Minutes later the ship shudders, and a calm voice fills the address system. Passengers must stay in their seats while the subspace drive is cut. George asks what is wrong, and Silvia snaps that she is no mechanic.
67633-history-of-the-1-4th-battalion-duk:
History of the 1/4th Battalion, Duke of Wellington West Riding Regiment, is a unit history of 1914 to 1919. Captain Bales, holder of the Military Cross and former adjutant, wrote the record. Mortimer of Halifax and London published the battalion story in 1920. It is dedicated to all ranks of the battalion who fell in action.

A preface tells how keeping the battalion war diary for two years suggested the history. Soon after the armistice Bales put the idea forward and carried it through. Photographs show the battalion in 1914 and the cloth hall at Ypres in 1918. Yorkshire Territorials gain their trench years preserved by their own diarist.
68253-thunder-in-the-void:
Thunder in the Void is a science fiction novel by Henry Kuttner. It first ran in Astonishing Stories in October 1942. An escaped convict opens the tale. Saul Duncan flees through an Arctic blizzard. He has broken out of the Transpolar Penitentiary. That fortress stands within the Arctic Circle. Guard planes patrol its frozen waste.

Only a blizzard hides a runner from those planes. A smuggled compass guides Duncan over the ice. Warmth steals over him, a sure sign of death. He fights it off and plows on. A voice in the motto vows to take a boat to Pluto. Many will die before that vow is done. Kuttner wrote pulp tales at a furious pace. Space war and prison planets are his ground here.
6836-three-men-and-a-maid:
Wodehouse opens Three Men and a Maid in a New York apartment rented by Mrs. Horace Hignett, where golden sunlight peeps through curtained windows like spies of an advancing army. Three clocks disagree: the Dutch clock says nine thirteen, the ormolu ten eleven, the carriage clock six fourteen, so it is exactly eight, and Mrs. Hignett, who always wakes at eight precisely, sits up in bed.

Mrs. Hignett, world-famous writer on theosophy, soon faces three men and a maid in a comic tangle of love, wills, and hotels. Wodehouse keeps the farce bright and the talk sharp. Three Men and a Maid is a gay, classic Wodehouse comedy of money, marriage, and mischief.
68418-problem-in-solid:
George Smith wrote a science fiction tale with art by Orban, printed in a magazine dated October 1947. Martin Hammer, the worlds top maker of moving pictures, should have been ready for anything at all. Earthquakes or fatherhood alike should not lift his brow, the tale jokes, yet Hammer had not seen everything yet.

A noise at his office door sounds like a dentists drill on wood, or a light scroll saw at work. A mans hand then comes through the door, gripping a knob that is not there, and swings a false door wide. The real door falls in fine sawdust as the guest steps through his own outline in the wood.
69338-the-moon-maid:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Moon Maid, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1926. Burroughs was already famous for the Tarzan books and the Martian stories. A prologue called The Message from Mars frames the tale, and part one follows the flight of the ship Barsoom to the Moon.

Inside the Moon, the voyagers find human quadrupeds and fall into the hands of the Va-gas. A lunar storm, an exodus, and a battle follow, and the Moon Maid herself escapes. The fight with the Kalkars and their city fills the later chapters. Part two, The Moon Men, jumps ahead to a conquest of Earth, with Julian the Eighth arrested and revolution brewing. Burroughs mixes hollow-Moon adventure with a dark future history of invasion.
71597-tattle-tales-of-cupid:
Paul Leicester Ford gathered his early love stories and two short plays in a volume issued at New York in 1898. A dedication letter to his childhood playmate explains the title: the two children invented their own stories together, preferring them to any in books. When she found a new playfellow, he played on alone.

The stories are His Version of It, A Warning to Lovers, Sauce for the Goose, and The Cortelyou Feud. The first opens on horses talking in their stalls, a bay mare and a carriage-horse agreeing that a certain lady is a darling. The plays, The Best Laid Plans and Man Proposes, close a book of courtship told lightly.
71781-the-poetical-works-of-janet-little:
Janet Little, known as the Scotch Milkmaid, published her poetical works at Air in 1792, printed by John and Peter Wilson. She inscribed the poems to Flora, Countess of Loudoun, as her ever grateful and obedient humble servant. A working dairy woman issuing a book of verse was a rarity worth the title page's pride.

Contents list poems To Hope, On Happiness, The Lottery Ticket, and The Month's Love, plus pastorals such as Damon and Philander and Colin and Alexis. One elegy personates a husband grieving for his wife. Another piece records a visit to Mr Burns. Readers get the verse of a labouring-class Scottish poet writing beside Burns in his own decade.
72392-the-inverted-pyramid:
The Inverted Pyramid is a novel by Bertrand Sinclair, published in Boston by Little, Brown in 1924. A line from Conrad stands at its head, on the warfare that fills the life-history of the earth. The scene is the Pacific coast of Canada.

The first chapter opens with an inventory. One boy of eighteen, Roderick Norquay. One girl of fifteen, Mary Thorn. One gaudy cedar dugout canoe, carved and painted in flaming red, blinding yellow, and piercing blue. One stretch of tide race running between an island shore and a rock-strewn point. Rod waits on the shore of Little Dent for the flood tide to strengthen. The narrator wonders why no poet has sung this swirling water, and no novelist made the north coast his stage.
72454-what-the-wind-did:
What the Wind Did is a tale by Amy Le Feuvre, author of Probable Sons and Teddy's Button. Copyright in 1899, it was issued by the Fleming H. Revell Company of New York, Chicago, and Toronto. The book is short, with five chapters, and most of them give one man's life story in his own words.

The tale opens with a young clerk in a country bank who walks to work each day at half past nine. On a wild wet March morning he sees a small girl fight the wind with a big umbrella. The wind snatches it, knocks her down, and spills her bag of books, and so the two meet.
72543-what-america-did:
What America Did, by Florence Finch Kelly, records what the United States achieved in carrying on the First World War. The book was published in New York in 1919, just after the fighting ended.

Kelly first treats the fighting forces on land, at sea, and in the air. Chapters cover making and housing the army, building a munitions industry from nothing, and caring for the wounded. A second part turns to the nation behind the fighters: paying for the war, the bridge of boats to France, and control of trade, fuel, and railroads. When the country entered the war in April 1917, Kelly notes, its whole army came to barely two hundred thousand men. The book measures how far the country travelled from that small start.
73173-einstein-s-planetoid:
Paul Dennis Lavond wrote a space tale that ran in Science Fiction Quarterly in the spring of 1942. Lavond was a name shared by three writers, Kornbluth, Lowndes, and Pohl, the notes say. The heirs of space flight plan to be the first humans to land on Alpha Centauri. But the first Hartnett expedition was lost, and they must find it first.

They follow signals to the screwiest planetoid in the galaxy, the blurb cries. Nick Hartnett steps off the lip of a thousand foot shaft and floats gently down into the lounge of the Columbia. Dorothy Gilbert lies curled in a spring hammock reading a book on orbits. Nick reads the title over her shoulder before she knows he has come in. Lost ships and bent space drive the tale.
73421-be-not-afraid:
Be Not Afraid gathers stories from the New Testament by Catharine Shaw. Shaw had writ Cherry's Choice and Mother's Bible Stories before this book. John Shaw and Company of London printed this copy in the year 1928. A picture called Sowing and Reaping stands at the front of the work. The contents list runs past forty short pieces for young readers here.

Four opening pieces retell the Sermon on the Mount in plain parts. How to live and how to pray fill those first sermon chapters. The Last Supper, Peter's denial, and the risen Saviour's pardon follow on. No room at the inn, the lilies, and a man named Matthew appear. Calvary, the Good Shepherd, and the lost sheep fill the mid list. Parables of the two builders, ten virgins, and tares close the set. Shaw retells each tale in short words for children at home.
73952-the-voice-of-the-void:
John Campbell wrote a short space tale on the far reaches of matter and force. The tale ran in Amazing Stories Quarterly in the summer of 1930. Wesso drew the pictures for it. A front note praises Campbell as a young fan choice. It says his tale weaves high science with bold deeds.

Stars are so far that light years are the yard stick here. In suns, atoms split to yet more small bits of stuff. Mass and force trade places in a strange round. A strange small man stands at the tale's core. Readers get big thought in a short, tense frame.
74939-a-little-maid:
Amy Le Feuvre's A Little Maid, issued in London by the Religious Tract Society in 1905, opens on a doorstep in Bone Alley, in the slums. Peggy, a thin girl in a faded blue felt hat with a ragged crow's feather, hugs her knees among orange peel and broken bottles. She scolds herself for dreaming too high.

The chapter heads carry her into service with her aunt, through country mud, a heathen stocking, and a spell as a real little home missionary. Sydney Cowell drew the three illustrations, including the frontispiece scene of a stranger asking the little girl what is the matter and whether she cannot get a place.
77575-the-indiscretions-of-a-lady-s-maid:
The Indiscretions of a Lady's Maid is a novel by William Le Queux, the writer billed in his publisher's pages as the Master of Mystery. Pages of press praise open the volume, gathered from papers across Britain. The Pall Mall Gazette says he whirls readers from incident to incident without pause for thought.

The Daily Graphic calls his illusion correct and leaves readers panting for more. The Review of Reviews rates him an adept at the semi-detective story. The Daily Mail names his books the best companion on a railway trip, and the Scotsman finds them delightfully convincing. The Northern Whig says he has brought the sensational novel to high perfection. Such billing matches the title: a maid's indiscretions, told at speed, with a mystery at the core.
77658-the-cybernetic-kid:
John Jakes tells a comic tale of Fred Ajax, whose Ajax Enterprises is nearly broke after his Skin-of-Delight lamp ran its course and monthly bills finished the job. Walking through a city park with Sailor Burns, a wrestler known across the system from telecasts, Ajax cannot see why something keeps striking the Sailor's knobby head. The trouble is a boy of about eight with crew-cut hair and large glasses, firing a pea-shooter from the shrubbery.

The boy waves the weapon in derision, but called out, he answers in grown-up language: he was only seeking a little relaxation. The magazine's headnote gives the premise plainly. A child genius is like an atomic acorn, able to grow into a sturdy oak or blow the lid off generally. Ajax, badly in need of an angle before the creditors act, has just met one.
77744-songs-of-the-unblind-cupid:
Songs of the Unblind Cupid, by Lloyd, is a small book of love poems from 1899. Lloyd also wrote Wind Harp Songs and The Red Heart in a White World. A verse at the front asks Cupid if his blinders are off at last. Sing, laddie, sing, snap the music blithe and free from the bold bowstring.

You will be a man now, you will see why, that opening song goes on. Every lass shall have her right and no lass shall cry, it vows in rhyme. The Cactus Flower is the first poem in the book after the song. A woman comes brimming with love, a red cactus flower filled with dew, there. Free love and free thought verse of the 1890s fills this odd little volume.
784-boyhood-in-norway-stories-of-boy-lif:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen wrote these stories of boy life in Norway, the land of the midnight sun. Tales such as The Battle of the Rafts, The Clash of Arms, and Biceps Grimlund's Christmas Vacation follow lads at school, on farms, and by fjords. Snow, boats, and hard play shape their days.

Boyesen, himself Norwegian-born, writes with warmth for the old country and its customs, from Christmas feasts to tales of Vikings retold by boys. The stories praise pluck, fair play, and loyalty, without hiding the cold or the risk. The book gives young readers a vivid, affectionate tour of Norway as it was.
8730-a-little-bush-maid:
Mary Grant Bruce introduces Norah, a girl growing up on Billabong. A station in northern Victoria so large she can ride all day and never see anyone she does not want to see. Pets and playthings, a menagerie race, Jim's idea, anglers' bend. A bush fire fill the early chapters, before a murder at Winfield, a circus, camping out, and a fight against death raise the stakes. The final chapters bring evening and the end of the struggle.

Bruce writes the Australian bush as a place of freedom and hard work, where a girl can ride, fish, and face danger on equal terms with boys. The Billabong books became beloved Australian children's classics, and this first volume sets their pattern: station life, loyal friends. A heroine whose courage is practical rather than showy. Young readers still enjoy Norah's adventures, and older ones find a warm picture of rural Australia.
8994-what-katy-did:
Susan Coolidge wrote this children's classic about Katy Carr, a tall, high-spirited girl who longs to be good and beautiful but keeps falling into scrapes. After a swing accident leaves her hurt and shut indoors, Katy must learn patience, unselfishness, and the quiet heroism of bearing pain well. Her family and her wise cousin help her on the way.

Coolidge dedicates the book to five children who once played beneath green boughs, now grown. The tale's warmth, humor, and moral sense made Katy a beloved figure for generations of girls. It still charms as a story of growing up, not by grand deeds but by small, daily choices.
9070-the-imaginary-invalid:
Molière wrote this comedy in French as Le Malade imaginaire, and Charles Heron Wall turned it into English prose. It was the last play Molière wrote, first acted in Paris on February 10, 1673, with Molière himself playing Argan, the hero. Argan thinks he is sick and spends his days counting his apothecary's bills.

His wife schemes for his money, his daughter loves a young man her father rejects, and doctors and quacks crowd the house with cures. The jokes bite at doctors who profit from fear, and at patients who love their ills. It remains one of Molière's funniest plays, sharp, fast, and full of stage life.
a-little-bush-maid: Mary Grant Bruce tells of a little bush maid at Billabong station in Victoria. Norah's home is so large that one could ride all day and never see anyone unwelcome. Chapters follow pets, a menagerie race, a bush fire, fishing, and a circus. Bruce writes an Australian girls story of station life and friendship.
a-sweet-little-maid: Amy Ella Blanchard tells the story of another sweet little maid in this book, lovingly dedicated to her goddaughter Agnes Blanchard Williams. The contents run from Dimple and Bubbles and dolls through a quarrel, housebreakers, a tea party, and housekeepers to being adrift, downtown, a picnic, and an uncle and a wedding. Copyrighted in 1899, it belongs with the author's other little miss and mistress stories for young readers.
an-old-maid:
Honoré de Balzac sets his novel in Alençon, a quiet French town, where the rich and aging Mademoiselle Cormon wishes at last to marry. Her choice of husband becomes the town's great contest. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the book, as its title page states. Two rivals scheme for her hand and her fortune.

Seven chapters follow the Chevalier de Valois, the scheming du Bousquier, and the gentle young Athanase, who loves her in silence. Balzac mixes comedy about provincial manners with a sadder look at pride, gossip, and wasted hope. The ending, named in the contents as a final disappointment, lands with real sting.
boyhood-in-norway-stories-of-boy-life-in:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen, a Norwegian immigrant who became an American professor, wrote Boyhood in Norway as linked stories of boy life in the land of the midnight sun. The Battle of the Rafts opens the book with a deadly feud between East-Side and West-Side boys in Numedale. Rafts, ambushes, and thrashings follow the rules of boy warfare.

Other tales give Biceps Grimlund's Christmas vacation, a masquerade, the story of a horse, and Bonnyboy, plus a bear that had a bank account. Boyesen writes from his own Norwegian childhood, keeping the scenery, school customs, and sagas in the background. The stories balance mischief with moral consequence, and preserve a rural Norway of the 1850s.
britannica-1911-abd-ul-mejid:
Abd-ul-Mejid receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abd-ul-Mejid, sultan of Turkey, was born in 1823 and succeeded his father Mahmud the Second in 1839. Defeat at Nezib and a fleet handed to Mehemet Ali met him at his accession; European hands saved the empire.

Reform was his father's charge, and the Hatt-i-sherif of Gulhané in 1839 promised life, property, fair taxes, and equal rights for all subjects. A second edict followed the Crimean War in 1856. Army, schools, and tax reform moved slower than paper, against ulema and governing-class resistance. Kossuth's refugees found a bold protector in him. Kind and honourable but weak and extravagant, the entry judges. Reckless foreign loans of his reign led toward default.
britannica-1911-abercromby-david:
David Abercromby receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. Abercromby, a seventeenth-century Scottish physician, won note enough for his Nova Medicinae Praxis to be reprinted at Paris in 1740, long after his likely death. Venereal cure without mercury made his Latin fame in 1684.

Pulse variation and a plant-tasting guide to drug powers fill his medical shelf, gathered as Opuscula in 1687. Theology claims the larger fame: bred a Jesuit at Douai, he turned Protestant and wrote Protestancy proved Safer than Popery. A Discourse of Wit of 1685 holds early, sharp marks of the Scottish common-sense school. A moral treatise on interest, offered to Boyle, followed. Haller's bibliography keeps his medical name.
britannica-1911-acetic-acid:
Acetic acid is one of the most important organic acids, the sharp substance that makes vinegar sour. It occurs in the juice of many plants, but people obtain it mainly by oxidizing spoiled wines or by distilling wood destructively. The ancients knew it as vinegar, and Lavoisier showed late in the eighteenth century that air is needed to turn alcohol into vinegar. Kolbe's synthesis of a related acid provided the first full synthesis of acetic acid itself.

Properties and uses fill the entry. Pure, or glacial, acetic acid forms leafy crystals, melts just above sixteen degrees, and smells exceedingly pungent. Its salts, the acetates, serve as mordants in dyeing, as sugar of lead, and as verdigris pigment, and doctors used acetates to raise the blood's alkalinity.
britannica-1911-acid:
Acid, from a Latin root meaning sharp or sour, names any sour substance loosely, but chemistry gives the word a precise sense. An acid is a substance containing hydrogen that metals can replace, forming salts, so an acid may be viewed as a salt of hydrogen. Acids dissolve alkalies and many metals, neutralize alkaline substances, and redden blue vegetable colourings such as litmus.

Theory has a long history here. The ancients knew vinegar, Paracelsus imagined a souring principle, and Boyle fixed the tests of litmus and salt formation. Lavoisier wrongly made oxygen the acid-producing element in all acids. The entry then treats organic acids, marked by the carboxyl group, their classification, and their reactions into salts, esters, chlorides, and amides.
britannica-1911-baird-sir-david:
Baird, Sir David (1757-1829), was a British general. He was born at Newbyth in Aberdeenshire. He joined the army in 1773. India received him in 1779. He served as captain in the Highlanders there. Hyder Ali's forces destroyed his detachment soon after.

Baird fell wounded into Mysore hands. The prisoners suffered barbarous treatment. They stayed captive over four years. His wound's bullet came out only at release. Baird rose fast after that ordeal. He fought Tippoo under Cornwallis in 1792. He served at the Cape of Good Hope too. In 1799 he led the storming party at Seringapatam. The stronghold had once held him prisoner. Parliament and the East India Company thanked him. A pension was offered and declined. He hoped for the order of the Bath instead.
britannica-1911-bayazid:
Bayazid, or Bajazet, is a border fortress town of Asiatic Turkey, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands near the frontiers of Russia and Persia, at about 6000 feet, looking across a marshy plain to the great cone of Ararat. The town sits in a bowl of sharp, rocky hills, on the site of the old Armenian town of Pakovan. 

A palace crowns the account. On a knoll stands the half-ruined palace of past governors, built for Mahmud Pasha by a Persian architect. It is held one of the finest buildings in Turkey. The town holds two churches and a monastery famed for age and grandeur. Its people had shrunk to about 4000. Russia took the place in 1828, in 1854, and again in 1878. The Turks then won it back and besieged the Russian garrison. Relief came, but a massacre of Christians followed.
britannica-1911-beaton-david:
David Beaton, a Scottish cardinal and archbishop of Saint Andrews who lived from about 1494 to 1546, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a younger son of John Beaton of Balfour in the county of Fife. He was educated at the universities of Saint Andrews and Glasgow. In his sixteenth year he was sent to Paris, where he studied civil and canon law.

About that time Beaton was presented to the rectory of Campsie by his uncle James Beaton, then archbishop of Glasgow. When his uncle moved to Saint Andrews in 1522, he resigned the rich abbacy of Arbroath in favour of his nephew. The great ability of Beaton and the backing of his uncle ensured his rapid rise in church and kingdom.
britannica-1911-benzoic-acid:
Benzoic acid is the simplest of the aromatic acids, a family of ring-shaped sour compounds. It occurs in nature in some resins, above all gum benzoin, in dragon’s blood, and bound up in the Peru and Tolu balsams. Chemists prepare it by oxidising toluene, benzyl alcohol or benzaldehyde, among many other routes the entry lists.

The acid forms glistening leaf-like crystals from water and melts at a low, exact heat. A large family of its children follows in the article: benzoic anhydride, benzoyl chloride, ethyl benzoate and benzamide, each with its making and marks. Medicine uses the salts, above all ammonium benzoate, as a wash against infection in the bladder and kidneys.
britannica-1911-blondel-david:
Blondel, David is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French Protestant clergyman. He was born at Chalons-sur-Marne in 1591 and died on the sixth of April 1655. In 1650 he followed Vossius as professor of history at Amsterdam. His works were very many.

In some of them he showed a rare critical gift. The best known is his study of Pope Joan, printed in 1647 and again in 1657. In it he reached the finding, now held by all, that the tale of a female pope is a mere myth. That finding stirred strong anger among Protestants of his day. The entry is short, but it marks Blondel as a scholar who let the evidence rule, even when his own side disliked the result.
britannica-1911-butyric-acid:
Butyric acid is a fatty acid found in butter and in the sweat and fluids of the flesh. The 1911 Britannica article says two acids share its formula, the normal kind and the iso kind. The normal acid shows in the oil of a giant hogweed and in parsnip roots. In the lab it is most often made by the souring of sugar or starch. Rotting cheese is added to start the change, with chalk to tame the acids formed.

The acid is an oily liquid with a foul smell. It turns solid at a cold well below the freeze point of water, and it boils at a high heat. It mixes with ease in water and in alcohol. Strong agents burn it down to carbon dioxide and acetic acid. The iso kind is found free in carob pods and in arnica root, and in croton oil in bound form.
britannica-1911-calderwood-david:
David Calderwood (1575–1650) was a Scottish divine and church historian. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was educated at Edinburgh and took his degree in 1593. About 1604 he became minister of Crailing, near Jedburgh. There he opposed the push to introduce Episcopacy. In 1617 a Remonstrance from the Presbyterian clergy reached his hands. The king examined him at St Andrews about it. Calderwood would not surrender the list of signatures.

Punishment followed his defiance of King James. He lost his charge and was jailed. The privy council ordered him banished from the kingdom. In August 1619 he sailed for Holland. There he published his Altare Damascenum. He returned to Scotland in 1624 and took the parish of Pencaitland. His last years went to a History of the Church of Scotland. The General Assembly voted him a pension to finish it. The work survives as a rich storehouse of source material.
britannica-1911-carbolic-acid:
Carbolic acid, or phenol, is a chemical from coal-tar. Its formula is C6H5OH, and its name is hydroxy-benzene. This long 1911 Britannica article gives its sources and making. It occurs in the urine of grass-eating animals. It is also found in small quantity in castoreum. Runge discovered it in coal-tar in 1834. The tar fraction boiling between 150 and 200 degrees holds it.

The article explains how the phenol is won from that fraction. Caustic soda is used to dissolve the phenol out. Water then throws down the tar hydrocarbons mixed with it. Acid frees the phenols, which rise as an oily layer. Careful distillation then recovers the pure phenol. It can also be made in the laboratory by other routes. Fusing a benzene sulphonate with alkali is one route named. The article goes on to its reactions and its many uses.
britannica-1911-carbonic-acid:
Carbonic acid forms when carbon dioxide dissolves in water. Its proper formula is H2CO3. This very short 1911 Britannica entry defines the term. Its salts are called carbonates by chemists. The name carbonic acid is also used more loosely. It is often given to carbon dioxide itself, the neutral gas.

That loose use rests on two grounds given in the entry. The gas forms salts with oxides, like an acid. Its solution in water also shows an acid nature. The entry admits the loose use is not systematic. Still, it notes that the practice is very common. The whole notice runs to a few lines only. It gives the formula, the salts, and the naming point. Readers are left with a precise definition and a warning.
britannica-1911-cardioid:
The cardioid is a curve in mathematics. Its name comes from the Greek kardia, meaning heart. Castillon named it for its heart-like form. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its properties. Louis Carré treated it mathematically in 1705. Koersma also worked on it in 1741. It is a particular form of the limaçon curve. It can be made as an epicycloid with equal circles.

The cardioid can also be seen as an inverse parabola. It arises as a caustic curve in optics as well. That caustic comes from rays reflected at a spherical surface. The rays start from a point on the circumference. Its polar equation is r = a(1 + cos θ). The curve is symmetric about its initial line. It has a cusp at the origin of the figure. Its area is one and a half times the generating circle's area. The length of the whole curve is 8a.
britannica-1911-cichlid:
Cichlid (Cichlidae) are a family of fishes related to the perches and wrasses, confined to fresh and brackish waters of Central and South America, Africa, Syria, India and Ceylon. Many new genera and species, some with strange changes in their teeth, have lately been found in tropical Africa. The great lakes Victoria, Tanganyika and Nyasa supply many of those finds. About 180 species are known from Africa, 150 from America and three from India and Ceylon.

Nursing habits make the family remarkable, since parents shelter eggs and young inside the mouth and throat. Old reports gave that care to the male, but long observation shows it falls invariably on the female in African and Syrian species. Named cases once credited to males proved, on examination of the glands, to be females. Eggs vary hugely, from 100 to 200 in some kinds to only four very large eggs in Tropheus moorii.
britannica-1911-cinnamic-acid:
Cinnamic acid, also called phenylacrylic acid, is the subject of a science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The acid is found, in the form of one of its salts, in Peru and Tolu balsams, in storax, and in some gum benzoins. The entry lists several ways to make it in the lab. The most used route is the one named for Perkin.

The article walks through that process step by step. Certain starting goods are heated for some hours to a high heat. The mix is then made alkaline, steam drives off the excess of one part, and the clear fluid is treated with a strong acid. The cinnamic acid then falls out as a solid, and it can be cleaned by dissolving it again in hot water. The entry notes past dispute over how the change works, settled by the work of Fittig and his pupils.
britannica-1911-citric-acid:
Citric acid, or oxytricarballylic acid, is a tetrahydroxytribasic acid first obtained in solid state by Karl Wilhelm Scheele in 1784 from lemon juice. It is present also in oranges, citrons, currants, gooseberries and many other fruits, and in several bulbs and tubers. Large scale making starts from lime or lemon juice, or from fermenting glucose with named ferments. About 20 gallons of lemon juice should yield about 10 pounds of crystallised acid.

The making runs through calcium citrate, split by dilute sulphuric acid, then filtered and concentrated, preferably in vacuum pans.
